cues.text: Section nine: IT project management and implementation.
A note before we begin.
This section is in the textbook, even though the LMS Part A and Part B readings do not cover it.
A project is a temporary effort to deliver a defined outcome.
IT project management coordinates scope, time, cost, quality, resources, risks and stakeholders.
Implementation converts plans into operational systems, through development, testing, deployment and adoption.
Ongoing operation after handover is distinct from the project itself.
Now, why does project management matter?
There are five reasons.
First, complexity.
There are dependencies between applications, vendors, infrastructure and teams.
Second, time and budget.
Projects need realistic schedules, sensible resource allocation, and monitoring of variance.
Third, alignment.
Requirements and deliverables must serve the business objective.
Fourth, risk.
We must anticipate integration failure, scope changes, resource shortages and vendor delays.
And fifth, communication.
Users, executives, technical staff and suppliers all need to be coordinated.
The benefits include improved delivery success, more efficient use of resources, better quality and customer satisfaction, and better handling of change.
A multinational ERP rollout illustrates the importance of requirements analysis, phased deployment, training and post-launch monitoring.
Let us now look at three approaches, beginning with Waterfall.
Waterfall is a sequential approach with defined phases: requirements, then design, then implementation, then testing, then deployment, and finally maintenance.
Each phase establishes its deliverables before the next one proceeds.
Its advantages are clear milestones, thorough documentation, and predictable planning when requirements are stable.
Its disadvantages are late feedback, expensive changes, and the potential for usability problems to be discovered late.
It is appropriate for well-defined projects with strong documentation needs.
Note that in practice, change can be controlled rather than literally impossible.
Next, Agile.
Agile is an iterative and incremental approach.
It delivers usable portions of a product, obtains feedback, and adapts.
Iterative means revisiting and improving; incremental means adding functionality in pieces.

Agile emphasises people and collaboration, working software, customer involvement, and responsiveness to change, while still recognising the importance of processes, documentation, contracts and plans.
Short cycles allow early feedback, and they reduce the cost of discovering mistaken assumptions.
The advantages are adaptability, early value, regular testing and collaboration.
The challenges are that it requires disciplined prioritisation, stakeholder participation, and management of scope creep.
Agile is not permission to abandon planning or documentation.
Finally, Scrum.
Scrum is a framework within Agile, not a competing philosophy.
It organises work in time-boxed sprints.
The course describes typical sprints of two to four weeks.
Scrum defines three accountabilities, and the table has one row for each.
The Product Owner has the purpose of maximising product value and ordering the product backlog.
The Scrum Master helps the team use Scrum effectively and address impediments.
And the Developers are cross-functional team members who create a usable increment.
Scrum also has four events.
Sprint Planning establishes a goal and a work plan.
The Daily Scrum inspects progress and adapts the plan.
The Sprint Review inspects outcomes with stakeholders.
And the Sprint Retrospective improves how the team works.
The Sprint itself contains all of these events.
Lastly, three terms to keep apart.
The product backlog is the ordered work for the product.
The sprint backlog is the sprint goal plus the selected work, with a delivery plan.
And the increment is the usable result that meets the Definition of Done.
